pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 2: Algorithm

In this unit you will write complete algorithms using both flowcharts and pseudocode, including sequence, selection and iteration, and translate between the two formats.

pages.title: Content standard and lessons
pages.body:
> 🎯 **Content standard**
- **B9.4.2.1** Analyse the correct step-by-step procedure in solving any real-world problem.

> 🧭 **What you will be able to do**
- **B9.4.2.1.1** Write a program using flowchart and pseudocode algorithms that include sequence, selection and iteration.
- **B9.4.2.1.2** Translate a flowchart algorithm into pseudocode and vice versa.

> 🗺️ **Lessons in this unit**
- 13.1 Writing Algorithms with Flowcharts and Pseudocode
- 13.2 Translating Between Flowcharts and Pseudocode

**Core competencies developed:** Creativity and Innovation (CI6.1, CI5.4), Critical Thinking (CP6.4).

pages.title: Writing Algorithms with Flowcharts and Pseudocode
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.4.2.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- discuss at least three ways of hand-washing and preparing beverages;
- write algorithms focused on correctness and shortest execution time.
**Pseudocode** is a way of writing an algorithm in structured, plain English using keywords such as INPUT, OUTPUT, IF … THEN … ELSE … ENDIF, WHILE … ENDWHILE, REPEAT … UNTIL and FOR … NEXT. It is not a real programming language, but it can easily be turned into code.
| **Three ways to wash/clean hands** | **Notes** |
|---|---|
| Soap and running water (tap) | Rub all parts of the hands for at least 20 seconds; rinse; dry |
| Veronica bucket (soap and water from a bucket with a tap) | Common in Ghanaian schools, markets and homes; the waste water collects in a basin |
| Alcohol-based hand sanitiser | When soap and water are not available; rub until dry (about 20–30 seconds); not effective on visibly dirty hands |
[[fig:c9-f16|Figure 15: Flowchart for hand-washing, with selection and iteration]]
> ✏️ **Worked example — Pseudocode: hand-washing**
BEGIN
IF running water available THEN
use tap
ELSE
use Veronica bucket
ENDIF
wet hands; apply soap
count ← 0
REPEAT
rub palms, backs, between fingers, thumbs and nails
count ← count + 1 // seconds
UNTIL count ≥ 20
rinse hands; dry with clean towel
END

pages.title: Writing Algorithms with Flowcharts and Pseudocode (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c9-f17|Figure 16: Flowchart for preparing a beverage with or without sugar and milk]]
> ✏️ **Worked example — Pseudocode: beverage with or without sugar and/or milk**
BEGIN
INPUT sugar, milk
boil water; add tea or cocoa
IF sugar = "yes" THEN add sugar ENDIF
IF milk = "yes" THEN add milk ENDIF
stir
OUTPUT "Beverage ready"
END
## Correctness and shortest execution time
- **Correctness:** the algorithm must give the right result for **every** possible input (e.g. it must work whether or not water is running, and for every combination of sugar and milk: 4 possibilities).
- **Efficiency:** avoid unnecessary steps; do not repeat checks; do slow tasks in parallel where possible (e.g. boil water while fetching the cup and sugar).
- **Test** your algorithm by **dry-running** it with each set of inputs in a **trace table**.
> 🧪 **Activity**
Write a flowchart and pseudocode for **preparing Hausa koko or porridge** with options for sugar, milk and groundnuts. Then dry-run it for two different customers and check it gives the correct result.

pages.title: Translating Between Flowcharts and Pseudocode
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.4.2.1.2
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- convert a flowchart to pseudocode;
- convert pseudocode to a flowchart.
| **Flowchart symbol** | **Pseudocode equivalent** |
|---|---|
| Oval: Start / Stop | BEGIN / END |
| Parallelogram: input / output | INPUT x / OUTPUT x |
| Rectangle: process | total ← a + b |
| Diamond with two exits | IF condition THEN … ELSE … ENDIF |
| Diamond with a flow line looping back | WHILE condition … ENDWHILE or REPEAT … UNTIL condition |
> ✏️ **Worked example — Pseudocode to flowchart: average of class scores**
BEGIN
total ← 0
FOR i ← 1 TO 10
INPUT score
total ← total + score
NEXT i
average ← total / 10
IF average ≥ 50 THEN OUTPUT "Class passed" ELSE OUTPUT "Class needs support" ENDIF
END
**Flowchart:** Start → process (total ← 0, i ← 1) → decision (i ≤ 10?) → Yes: input score → process (total ← total + score; i ← i + 1) → back to the decision; No: process (average ← total / 10) → decision (average ≥ 50?) → output message → Stop.
> 💻 **Practical session — Both directions**
(1) Convert the beverage flowchart above into pseudocode **without looking** at the given answer, then compare. (2) Draw the flowchart for the “average of class scores” pseudocode. (3) Write pseudocode and a flowchart for a program that inputs a number and outputs whether it is **even or odd** (use number MOD 2 = 0).

pages.title: Review: written and practical tasks
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Write pseudocode that inputs three numbers and outputs the largest.
2. Draw a flowchart for a program that outputs the numbers 2, 4, 6 … 20.
3. Translate the hand-washing flowchart into pseudocode using a WHILE loop instead of REPEAT … UNTIL.
